structure.title: Higher Education in Colombia and the SPP Program (Section II)
Absolute and Relative Economic Mobility Results (Sections IV.B-E)
Outcome Heterogeneity by Baseline Characteristics (Section IV.F)
The Role of College Quality / Program Value-Added (Section IV.G)
Efficiency: Crowd-Out and Spillover Difference-in-Differences Check (Section V)
Marginal Value of Public Funds Cost-Benefit Analysis (Section VI)

observations.statement: States the causal estimand as the effect of financial-aid eligibility on later educational and labor-market outcomes, identified through two separate cutoffs, a test-score cutoff and a household-wealth cutoff, rather than a single running variable.

Explains that although the two eligibility rules jointly define a multidimensional discontinuity, the authors collapse each design into a univariate distance-to-cutoff measure and estimate each cutoff separately rather than pooling them into one weighted estimate.

Argues that manipulation of the running variables is implausible because program eligibility was announced only after the qualifying exam had already been taken and scored, treated as the basis for quasi-random assignment near both cutoffs.
observations.quote: the announcement of SPP came as a surprise

observations.statement: Names a second, complementary design, a decile-by-cohort difference-in-differences comparison of test-score deciles before and after the reform, used to test for spillovers onto non-recipients rather than to estimate the main treatment effect.

Lists six linked administrative sources spanning exam records, a household means-testing registry, financial-aid recipient records, postsecondary enrollment and completion records, a college graduation exam, and social-security payroll records, each attributed to a specific government agency.

States the exam cohorts and calendar coverage window for each data source, spanning several years before the policy through roughly a decade after high school completion, so that later-life outcomes can be tracked.

Reports that a small share of exam takers with prior college experience are dropped from the estimation sample, justifies the exclusion as necessary to isolate first-time college-going decisions, and reports the resulting sample counts by eligibility group.

Restricts one earnings comparison to a single graduation cohort rather than pooling cohorts, explaining in a footnote that a pandemic-era disruption specific to the other cohort would otherwise contaminate the later-life earnings measure, with an appendix figure shown as a check.

Defines each running variable as the signed distance of a student's exam score or wealth index from its eligibility threshold, with the wealth threshold itself varying by the student's residential area type.

Distinguishes program eligibility, the sharp assignment variable used for reduced-form estimates, from actual benefit receipt, the fuzzy first-stage variable, so that instrumental-variable estimates rescale reduced-form coefficients by the take-up rate rather than assume full compliance.

Constructs the skill-development outcome by summing scores on the generic-competency modules of the mandatory college graduation exam and standardizing the resulting index against a fixed reference cohort so that scores are comparable across exam years.

Expresses the earnings outcome in units of the contemporaneous monthly minimum wage rather than nominal currency, with zeros assigned to individuals without formal employment, and justifies the unit choice by the minimum wage's role in local wage setting.

Builds college value-added measures for learning and earnings separately by regressing pre-policy outcomes on program fixed effects together with a dense set of baseline controls, so a program's estimated fixed effect is interpreted as its contribution net of student selection.

Reports each main RD table with the reduced-form coefficient and its standard error stacked in adjoining rows, the control-group mean of the dependent variable, the selected local-polynomial bandwidth, and the effective number of control and treated observations used by the estimator.

States in the table notes that standard errors follow the named RD software's conventional local-linear output, and directs readers to a shared notes paragraph under the first table for formatting conventions reused across later tables.

Separates reduced-form intention-to-treat tables from a distinct instrumental-variable table that rescales the same outcomes by the first-stage take-up rate, presenting the two as complementary rather than substitute estimates.

Organizes outcome tables into panels defined by which running variable is used, so the same set of columns is estimated twice, once restricted to the low-wealth subsample and once to the high-test-score subsample.

Does not state an explicit clustering level or discuss why observations might be correlated within groups; standard errors are attributed only to the RD estimation command's default variance calculation.

Mentions a marginally significant coefficient using a p-value when describing the timing of the earnings effect, without a broader discussion of multiple-testing concerns despite estimating many outcomes across several tables.

For the difference-in-differences spillover check, uncertainty is shown only as confidence bands in coefficient plots rather than tabulated, with no separate discussion of the clustering or variance assumption used to build the bands.

Reports a formal manipulation test of both running variables using a named local-polynomial density estimator, with the test discussion placed in the main-text narrative and the corresponding density plot in the online appendix.

Reports a joint covariate-balance test around both cutoffs in an appendix table, cited from the main text as support for the no-manipulation assumption rather than reproduced in full in the body of the paper.

Presents first-stage take-up results as a dedicated row in the instrumental-variable table alongside the reduced-form and IV coefficients for every outcome, rather than in a separate stand-alone first-stage table.

States that a bandwidth-sensitivity check is reported for all main outcomes in an online appendix, showing point estimates and confidence intervals remain stable across smaller and larger bandwidth choices, without reproducing the underlying figures in the main text.

Reports a secondary balance check that regresses a predicted outcome, built from a large set of baseline characteristics, on the running variable to test for endogenous selection among the subsample taking the later college exam, placing the result in an appendix table.

Cross-checks the difference-in-differences spillover analysis with an alternative specification using raw counts of students rather than shares, summarized as reaching the same qualitative conclusion and placed entirely in the appendix.

Repeats the college-exam skill-development analysis using a longer post-graduation window that includes exam sittings during and after the pandemic period, presenting it as a robustness variant of the primary shorter-window specification.

Checks the earnings result against an alternative comparison-cohort choice by including a cohort otherwise excluded from the primary earnings specification, reporting the alternative in an appendix figure as producing a similar pattern.

Summarizes subgroup analysis by baseline school disadvantage, sex, and parental education entirely in a brief main-text paragraph, with the full set of interacted estimates deferred to an appendix section rather than a main table.

Does not label the baseline-characteristic subgroup comparisons as prespecified or exploratory, presenting them as a descriptive extension of the main results rather than flagging them as a distinct hypothesis-testing exercise.

Frames the improvement in college value-added as the mechanism connecting the financial-aid shock to later skill and earnings gains, testing this by treating estimated program-level value-added as an outcome within the same RD design used for the main results.

Compares realized attainment and earnings effects against effects predicted purely from the estimated shift in college value-added, interpreting a gap between realized and predicted attainment as evidence of a channel beyond college quality alone.

Interprets the earnings effect relative to the control-group mean and separately benchmarks it against effect sizes reported by prior financial-aid studies, framing the result as larger than most previously documented earnings effects in that literature.

Expresses the skill-development effect in standard-deviation units of the standardized college exam score and separately as a share of the control-group mean, presenting both metrics side by side rather than choosing one.

Uses a formal cost-benefit framework to translate projected lifetime earnings gains and government outlays into a single willingness-to-pay-to-cost ratio, then compares that ratio against ratios computed for other national financial-aid programs in the literature.

Acknowledges that recording informal-sector work as zero earnings could bias the formal-earnings effect if control-group students disproportionately work informally, and argues the concern is limited by citing informality patterns among similarly high-achieving students.

Notes that endogenous selection into taking the later college graduation exam could bias the skill-development estimate if financial-aid-induced test takers differ systematically from those who would have taken the exam regardless, and characterizes the resulting estimate as a lower bound under one directional assumption about that selection.
Flags that a decomposition of the earnings gain attributable to measured skill improvement is non-causal and offered only as an illustrative back-of-envelope calculation, not a formal estimate.

Discusses generalizability by contrasting the program's mandatory, near-universal exit exam and existing means-testing infrastructure with settings where standardized testing or means-testing participation is voluntary, arguing this affects how transportable the take-up channel is to other countries.

Cautions that findings on the absence of adverse effects for non-recipient students may not extend to policies that also change admissions practices at the targeted colleges, since the studied program left admissions criteria unchanged.

Pairs nearly every main results figure with a companion panel comparing pre- and post-policy outcomes for the two socioeconomic groups, using a consistent shape-and-color legend across the whole results section.

Places a standard-error-in-parentheses convention beneath each coefficient throughout every results table, and repeatedly cross-references a single shared notes paragraph under the first table instead of restating the same explanatory text in later tables.
Labels every appendix table and figure with an A prefix and states, the first time an appendix item is cited, that all such items are hosted online rather than printed in the journal article.

Previews the paper's main qualitative findings on enrollment, attainment, skill development, and earnings within the introduction itself, before the design and data sections, rather than holding all findings for the results sections.

Orders the empirical narrative as institutional background, then data, then design and validity, before turning to results, placing the identification discussion ahead of the outcome tables rather than interleaving them.

Treats the crowd-out and spillover check on non-recipients as its own numbered section following the main mobility results rather than folding it into a general robustness section, framing it as an efficiency question distinct from the earlier equity results.

States that the underlying administrative microdata are proprietary and names the specific government agencies from which access would need to be requested, rather than describing the data as openly downloadable.

Points readers to a named external replication package hosted on a data repository for the code that reproduces every table and figure in the main text and appendices, cited by a persistent identifier rather than described inline.

Characterizes all six underlying data sources as government administrative records rather than survey-collected, commercial, or web-scraped data, consistent with the paper's broader description of proprietary agency microdata.

States that the study received approval from a named university's institutional review board, citing a specific protocol number in the acknowledgments, without mentioning a preregistered analysis plan for the empirical specifications.

concordance.paper_says: Reports RD estimates from a named local-polynomial RD command with a robust bias-corrected inference procedure, described as the primary estimator throughout the results tables.
concordance.card_shows: Records the RD specifications' estimator as local-polynomial RD via the rdrobust command (ids s1-s4).

concordance.paper_says: States that standard errors follow the RD command's conventional local-linear standard-error output without specifying a clustering variable.
concordance.card_shows: Records the first specification's standard-error type as robust with cluster_level null, and leaves se.type unset for the remaining RD specifications.

concordance.paper_says: States the value-added regression includes a program (college-major) fixed effect alongside a dense vector of baseline controls.
concordance.card_shows: Records the value-added specification's fixed effects as the program-code variable codigo_prog.

concordance.paper_says: States that bandwidths are selected by a data-driven optimal-bandwidth procedure built into the RD command, with sensitivity to the choice checked in an appendix.
concordance.card_shows: Records a bandwidth-selection diagnostic describing the same data-driven default procedure observed in the code.

concordance.paper_says: Names the comparison group explicitly as students who narrowly missed either eligibility cutoff.
concordance.card_shows: Leaves the comparison-group field unrecorded for every extracted specification.

concordance.paper_says: Lists the specific baseline demographic, household, and high-school covariates included in the value-added regression in a footnote.
concordance.card_shows: Leaves the controls-summary field unrecorded for the value-added specification, noting only that multiple lettered control-set variants exist.

concordance.paper_says: Does not describe any weighting scheme for the main RD or value-added regressions in the reviewed text.
concordance.card_shows: Leaves the weights field unrecorded (null) for every extracted specification.

concordance.paper_says: Reports manipulation-test results for both running variables using a named local-polynomial density estimator.
concordance.card_shows: Records two density-test diagnostics, one per running variable, matching the same test.
concordance.note: Also matches diagnostic x2, the companion density test for the other running variable.

concordance.paper_says: Reports the program take-up rate at each cutoff as the first-stage relationship between eligibility and benefit receipt, tabulated in the instrumental-variable table.
concordance.card_shows: Records a first-stage diagnostic using program-benefit receipt as the outcome of an RD regression on both running variables.

concordance.paper_says: States that a bandwidth-sensitivity appendix shows the main RD coefficients are stable across smaller and larger bandwidth choices for all outcomes.
concordance.card_shows: Records only a different bandwidth-related practice, holding the bandwidth fixed across heterogeneous subgroup comparisons rather than varying the bandwidth to test sensitivity of the main estimates.
concordance.note: The card's only bandwidth-robustness record documents a different practice than the paper's stated bandwidth-sensitivity appendix; the appendix scripts themselves were not among the files read for the card (partial coverage).

concordance.paper_says: Presents six main numbered tables and eleven main numbered figures in the body of the article, each with several sub-panels, plus numerous appendix tables and figures.
concordance.card_shows: Records one table and two figures as observed outputs, reflecting a partial code-reading pass that stopped after seven of roughly thirty-two script files.
concordance.note: Card extraction coverage is partial (see provenance.reading_notes), so the output-count difference likely reflects reading-budget limits rather than a substantive disagreement.

concordance.paper_says: Names six specific administrative agencies as data sources, describing the unit of observation and coverage period for each.
concordance.card_shows: Records only two generically named datasets referenced in the code, with type, access, and unit of observation left unresolved.

concordance.paper_says: Reports the size of the exam-taker population, the excluded subgroup, and each running-variable subsample directly in the data section.
concordance.card_shows: Leaves the sample field unrecorded for every extracted RD specification.

concordance.paper_says: Reports a second, appendix-based balance check that regresses a predicted outcome built from many baseline characteristics on the running variable to test for endogenous selection into the later exam-taking subsample.
concordance.card_shows: Does not record a balance-table diagnostic among the four extracted diagnostics (two density tests, bandwidth selection, first stage).

gaps: No explicit statement of a clustering level or a rationale for the chosen standard-error type beyond citing the RD command's default variance estimator; no wild-bootstrap, randomization-inference, or few-clusters discussion appears in the reviewed text.
No weak-instrument statistic (such as an F-statistic) is reported for the fuzzy RD/IV first stage beyond the first-stage coefficient row itself.
No discussion of multiple-hypothesis-testing correction despite many outcomes being estimated across six main tables and further appendix tables.
No preregistration or pre-analysis plan is mentioned; only institutional review board approval is stated in the acknowledgments.

The online appendices (A-D) referenced throughout for additional diagnostics, robustness checks, and heterogeneity results are not included in this text extraction, so their exact contents could not be verified directly and are recorded here only as the main text describes them.
No explicit statement of the statistical software version or a full list of packages used beyond the named RD and density-test procedures.

reading.note: Read the full main text from the title and abstract through the reference list (pages 1-47 of the extracted text). Page 48 is an empty trailing page produced by the form-feed count and contains no text. The paper's online appendices A-D are a separate document hosted on Harvard Dataverse and are not part of this PDF/text extraction, so appendix-only tables and figures are recorded here only as the main text describes them, not read directly.
